extracted.intended_audience: writers, literary critics, students of literature, and educated readers interested in standards for history, poetry, translation, and prose
extracted.subtask_description: Prescriptive critical observations about writing history, poetry, translation, and prose — what makes those genres effective or faulty, with examples and anti-patterns. Useful for critics, writers, and students seeking standards for good literary and historical writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: History must state adequate causes and show continuity
rubrics_metrics.description: I consider the two works of Sallust which have come down to us entire, as romances founded on facts; no adequate causes are stated, and there is no real continuity of action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid treating historical narrative as a loose romantic collection of incidents. A good history should identify and explain causes and present a coherent continuity of events rather than isolated anecdotes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorial stance must suit the historical aim (subjective vs objective)
rubrics_metrics.description: In Thucydides... it is Thucydides himself whom you read throughout... in Herodotus it is just the reverse. He has as little subjectivity as Homer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide whether the historian's reflective, interpretive voice (Thucydidean) or an objective, age-spirit-evoking narration (Herodotean) better serves the subject; be consistent about the degree of authorial presence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance philosophical analysis with factual narrative (avoid extremes)
rubrics_metrics.description: The difference between the composition of a history in modern and ancient times is very great; still there are certain principles upon which the history of a modern period may be written, neither sacrificing all truth and reality, like Gibbon, nor descending into mere biography and anecdote.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim to combine truthful, philosophically-informed interpretation with reliable narrative. Avoid rhetorical grandstanding that sacrifices truth, and also avoid mere episodic biography that lacks analytic insight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid prioritizing theatrical 'effect' over vivid truth (Gibbon's fault)
rubrics_metrics.description: He takes notice of nothing but what may produce an effect; he skips on from eminence to eminence, without ever taking you through the valleys between... all is scenical, and, as it were, exhibited by candlelight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't select only the most sensational or picturesque materials; provide the underlying texture and ordinary details that make historical reality vivid and believable rather than theatrical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good history should attempt to fathom ultimate causes
rubrics_metrics.description: I protest I do not remember a single philosophical attempt made throughout the work to fathom the ultimate causes of the decline or fall of that empire.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A historian should seek to explain underlying, ultimate causes of large events (political, social, cultural), not merely compile anecdotes or rhetorical sketches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain political/national character when interpreting decline
rubrics_metrics.description: The true key to the declension of the Roman empire... the imperial character overlaying, and finally destroying, the national character. Rome under Trajan was an empire without a nation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When diagnosing systemic decline, relate institutional forms (e.g., imperial structures) to national character and social foundations; identify how structural changes affected national cohesion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorial voice/egotism in poetry can be a virtue
rubrics_metrics.description: In the Paradise Lost--indeed in every one of his poems--it is Milton himself whom you see... it is a sense of this intense egotism that gives me the greatest pleasure in reading Milton's works.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A strong, personal authorial presence woven through characters and narrative can enrich poetry; the poet's distinctive voice perceived in multiple personae may be pleasurable and revealing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Skillful variation of a single image or motif
rubrics_metrics.description: Read particularly the Phoenix, and see how the single image of renascence is varied.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The ability to reproduce and vary the same central image or thought in different language is a mark of craft (as in Claudian and Pope); use variation to sustain and deepen a motif rather than repeat mechanically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid affectation; strive for individuality of character
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a great deal of affectation in Sterne, to be sure; but still the characters of Trim and the two Shandies are most individual and delightful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Excessive stylistic affectation weakens impact. Prioritize genuinely individual, well-delineated characters — individuality and truth of character can redeem stylistic oddities, but affectation alone undermines effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genius requires craft: pair high powers with technical skill
rubrics_metrics.description: Genius must have talent as its complement and implement, just as in like manner imagination must have fancy. In short, the higher intellectual powers can only act through a corresponding energy of the lower.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Large imaginative gifts must be matched by talent, technique, and craft (fancy, workmanship). Cultivate lower-order skills (diction, form, discipline) to let genius function effectively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral character matters for great poets
rubrics_metrics.description: There can be no great poet who is not a good man... His heart must be pure; he must have learned to look into his own heart, and sometimes to look at it; for how can he who is ignorant of his own heart know any thing of, or be able to move, the heart of any one else?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poetic greatness is tied to ethical inwardness: self-knowledge and moral seriousness enable a poet to move readers. This is a prescriptive aesthetic-moral standard for poetic stature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain elegance and correctness of diction
rubrics_metrics.description: I think there is a perceptible difference in the elegance and correctness of the English in our versions of the Old and New Testament. ... St. Paul is very often most inadequately rendered, and there are slovenly phrases which would never have come from Ben Jonson or any other good prose writer of that day.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strive for elegant, correct phrasing in translation and prose; avoid colloquial slovenliness in formal or literary contexts. Diction should reflect literary standards appropriate to the genre.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rhetorical passion must be grounded on calm, clear logic
rubrics_metrics.description: Irving's error to use declamation, high and passionate rhetoric, not introduced and pioneered by calm and clear logic, which is... like knocking a nail into a board, without wimbling a hole for it, and which then either does not enter, or turns crooked, or splits the wood it pierces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Warm rhetoric and passionate declamation need logical groundwork; build argumentative or emotional power on clear reasoned foundations to avoid ineffective or destructive rhetoric.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laughter arises from incongruous surprise (not contempt); manage danger for tone
rubrics_metrics.description: Aristotle's definition is as good as can be:--surprise at perceiving any thing out of its usual place, when the unusualness is not accompanied by a sense of serious danger. Such surprise is always pleasurable; and it is observable that surprise accompanied with circumstances of danger becomes tragic. Hence farce may often border on tragedy; indeed, farce is nearer tragedy in its essence than comedy is.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When writing comedy or farce, create pleasurable surprise without invoking real danger; if surprise includes danger, it tips toward the tragic. Use the degree of perceived danger to steer tonal outcome between farce, comedy, and tragedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer clarity and appropriate word-formation; avoid excessive compounding
rubrics_metrics.description: The old Latin poets attempted to compound as largely as the Greek; hence in Ennius such words as belligerentes, &c. In nothing did Virgil show his judgment more than in rejecting these... He saw that the Latin was too far advanced in its formation, and of too rigid a character, to admit such composition or agglutination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose lexical strategies suited to the language's stage and reader expectations. Overly agglutinated or compounded diction can impede clarity; judiciously prefer simpler or established forms to preserve elegance and readability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Translations should preserve original theological/semantic force
rubrics_metrics.description: We... ought surely to restore the Jehovah, and thereby bring out in the true force the overwhelming testimony of the Psalms to the divinity of Christ, the Jehovah or manifested God.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When translating, be mindful that particular lexical choices (e.g., proper names, divine titles) carry theological and rhetorical weight; preserving them can be necessary to convey the original's force and implications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain language competence through continual practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Hebrew is so simple, and its words are so few and near the roots, that it is impossible to keep up any adequate knowledge of it without constant application. The meanings of the words are chiefly traditional.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sustaining competence in a language (especially one with sparse lexicon/strong root-relations) requires continual study and use; expect traditional/conventional meanings and guard against erosion through neglect.
